shortDescription: Refresh the Shabab Balad investment case to scale learning-to-earning pathways and youth livelihoods
description: Technical assistance to strengthen the governance structure of the Shabab Balad board and its coalitions to ensure clear roles, accountability, and effective coordination across government, private sector, and UN partners. The assistance will also help develop a Monitoring and Evaluation framework with measurable indicators, clearly defined outcome pathways, and practical mechanisms to track progress and impact at scale. In addition, the TA will support the design of an integrated, government-led end-to-end pathway that links skills development with employability and entrepreneurship opportunities—including emerging sectors such as health, digital, green—ensuring that every young person—particularly girls, adolescents with disabilities, refugees, and those from underserved communities—can equitably and safely transition from learning to dignified and sustainable livelihoods.
objectives: "- Updated Shabab Balad investment framework - Updated governance documents for the board and coalitions with clarified roles, responsibilities, lines of accountability, and coordination mechanisms - M&E framework with measurable indicators, outcome pathways, data collection tools, and mechanisms for tracking performance and impact at scale - A fully developed, end-to-end pathways for the Nomu Al-Ghurair Program and Mastercard"

shortDescription: A strategic effort to expand El Salvador’s fiscal space through innovative financing, enabling a sustainable shift in how social programmes for children are fun

shortDescription: Yemen is conducting Groundwater potential mapping and would like oversight support and insights from lessons learnt in other countries
description:
The Minister of Water has requested UNICEF to develop an Integrated Watershed Management Plan for Taizz City. This task was broken down into 3 studies (i) a remote sending study to develop a groundwater potential map, (ii) an emergency well field and water supply infrastructure study, and (iii) the development of an Integrated Watershed Management Plan, building on the first 2 studies.
Under the UNICEF ToR for the Remote Sensing study, the primary scope was focused on remote sensing–based groundwater potential mapping. In a first step Acacia Water conducted a data gap analysis, including: (i) a clear overview of datasets to be used, (ii) verification of required data availability and quality, (iii) a structured data gap analysis, and (iv) recommendation for the way forward, was conducted through an existing standby agreement mechanism. The intention was to keep the assignment of the actual Remote Sensing study targeted, realistic and cost-efficient, with additional analytical layers potentially integrated in the actual Remote Sensing study.
The Ministry of Water has since proposed expanding the scope of the Remote Sensing study to include additional components: agricultural water demand assessment, surface runoff evaluation, land-use analysis and its impact on water use, climate change considerations, incorporation of existing groundwater monitoring data, and integration of water quality datasets. Given this expanded scope, we request: (1) an indication on associated costs for expanded scope; (2) Support with the technical evaluation of the proposals expected by the end of March, (3) sharing lessons learned and cost benchmarks from similar groundwater mapping initiatives in other country contexts to inform decision-making (4) Oversight support during implementation.
objectives: Groundwater Potential Maps for identified regions in Yemen

shortDescription: Institutionalize technology-enabled prevention and early intervention within national child protection systems
description:
A system-strengthening initiative to institutionalize technology-enabled prevention and early intervention services within national child protection systems. This includes digitizing Risiha assessment and case management tools and transitioning ParentText/ParentApp to government ownership. Embedding digitized Risiha tools into government and organisational service delivery will enable timely identification of risks, consistent monitoring, and improved targeting of support for vulnerable children and families. Concurrently, establishing governance and technical capacity for ParentText/ParentApp will ensure sustainability and scale-up of evidence-based digital parenting support. Together, these actions will reinforce national delivery of family-strengthening interventions to prevent violence in homes and communities.
Technical assistance is required to design and implement the digitization of Risiha tools, including technical specifications, integration with provincial and national IMS, data standards, workflows, and quality assurance. Additional support is needed to guide the government-led pathway to ownership of ParentText/ParentApp, covering governance structures, content stewardship, costed implementation plans, data protection protocols, and long-term systems integration. This assistance will build national capacity to sustain and scale both platforms, ensuring they function as core components of child protection systems for prevention and early intervention.
objectives:
Digitized Risiha tools designed and endorsed for roll-out at service delivery level, with district and provincial dashboards for reporting and planning
Agreed government ownership and transition framework for ParentText/ParentApp (Governance roles and quality standards agreed with government counterparts.)
Costed implementation roadmap for national scale-up of both platforms
TOR finalized for UNICEF resource overseeing RapidPro and digitized Risiha tools.
Draft costed roadmap for full government ownership of ParentText/ParentApp developed.
Data protection protocols reviewed and aligned with national child protection standards and POPIA.

shortDescription: Technical assistance to integrate climate‑sensitive water resources management into WASH programming
description:
This technical assistance will support UNICEF Yemen to strengthen the integration of climate‑sensitive water resources management (WRM) into WASH programme design, planning, and investment decisions. The TA will focus on improving the sustainability and resilience of groundwater‑dependent water supply systems by incorporating water availability assessments, climate risk screening of water sources, sustainable abstraction principles, and basic groundwater protection measures into WASH programming.
The assistance will help embed WRM considerations into technical designs, programme strategies, and planning tools, ensuring that WASH investments are aligned with long‑term water resource availability and climate resilience objectives. The TA will also provide technical guidance to support informed decision‑making in severely water‑scarce and climate‑stressed contexts, contributing to reduced risks of over‑abstraction, system failure, and unintended negative impacts on water resources.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables:
Practical guidance for integrating WRM into WASH programme design
Climate‑risk screening inputs for water supply interventions
Strengthened alignment between WASH investments and water resource sustainability
Enhanced technical capacity of staff and partners on WRM‑WASH linkages
objectives:
• Integrate climate‑sensitive water resources management principles into WASH programme design and planning
  • Improve the sustainability and resilience of groundwater‑dependent water supply systems
  • Strengthen climate risk screening and water availability considerations for WASH investments
  • Support alignment of WASH interventions with long‑term water resource protection and sustainability objectives under the CPD

shortDescription: Technical assistance on solarization and sustainability of water and sanitation systems under Yemen CPD 2027–2029
description:
This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen the design, sustainability, and climate resilience of water and sanitation systems through appropriate solarization and energy‑efficient technologies. The TA will focus on reducing reliance on fuel‑based systems, improving service continuity, and strengthening operation and maintenance (O&M) models for water supply and sanitation infrastructure in fragile and resource‑constrained contexts.
Support will include technical review and guidance on solar‑powered water supply systems, energy needs assessment, system sizing, lifecycle costing, and performance standards. In addition, the TA will provide technical inputs to improve the sustainability of sanitation systems, including wastewater management and fecal sludge treatment facilities, where energy requirements affect functionality and long‑term operation. The assistance will ensure that solarization contributes to climate mitigation and adaptation objectives while improving technical quality, cost‑effectiveness, and durability of WASH services.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables:

Technical guidance on solar‑powered water supply systems
Improved design and sustainability of energy‑dependent sanitation infrastructure
Lifecycle costing and O&M recommendations for solarized WASH systems
Strengthened technical capacity of staff and partners on solarization and sustainability
objectives:
• Improve technical quality and sustainability of solar‑powered water supply systems
  • Reduce dependency on fossil fuels for WASH service delivery
  • Strengthen lifecycle costing, O&M arrangements, and system performance
  • Enhance sustainability of sanitation and wastewater systems with energy requirements
  • Support alignment of WASH infrastructure with climate‑resilient and low‑carbon approaches

shortDescription: Technical assistance to strengthen sanitation and fecal sludge management (FSM) system
description:
This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen sanitation and fecal sludge management (FSM) systems in humanitarian, early recovery, and development contexts. The TA will focus on system‑based sanitation approaches, moving beyond isolated infrastructure to improved service chains from containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and safe disposal or reuse.
Support will include technical guidance on context‑appropriate FSM models for urban and small‑town settings, integration of sanitation into cholera prevention and epidemic preparedness strategies, and development of sustainable operation and maintenance arrangements. The TA will also address climate and environmental considerations, including flood‑resilient sanitation, safe sludge treatment, and reduction of environmental contamination, thereby strengthening public health and environmental outcomes.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables
Technical guidance on sanitation and FSM service‑chain design
Context‑appropriate sanitation and FSM models for fragile settings
Strengthened integration of sanitation into cholera prevention programming
Improved technical capacity of staff and partners on sanitation systems
objectives:
Strengthen sanitation programming through system‑based FSM approaches
Improve sustainability and functionality of sanitation services in urban and small‑town contexts
Integrate sanitation and FSM into cholera prevention and disease risk reduction strategies
Reduce environmental and public health risks associated with poor sanitationImprove technical quality and scalability of sanitation interventions under the CPD

shortDescription: Emergency‑to‑Systems (Humanitarian–Development Nexus WASH)
description:
This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen the transition of WASH programming in Yemen from short‑term emergency response to sustainable, systems‑based service delivery. The TA will focus on integrating humanitarian, development, and climate‑resilience approaches to reduce dependency on recurrent emergency interventions while maintaining life‑saving capacity.
Support will include technical guidance on designing WASH interventions that bridge immediate response and longer‑term sustainability, including service delivery models, operation and maintenance arrangements, institutional roles, and financing considerations suitable for fragile and conflict‑affected contexts. The assistance will also help align emergency WASH programming with CPD priorities on climate‑resilient systems, sustainability, and national capacity strengthening.
The technical assistance will also contribute to WASH‑for‑Peace efforts, particularly in Taiz, by strengthening systems‑based WASH approaches that reduce competition over scarce resources, support equitable service delivery, and reinforce confidence‑building between communities and local service providers. By promoting sustainable, shared, and well‑managed WASH services, the emergency‑to‑systems transition will support social cohesion objectives and help mitigate local tensions linked to water scarcity and service access.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables

Technical guidance on emergency‑to‑systems WASH transition models
Practical recommendations for nexus‑oriented WASH programme design
Improved alignment between humanitarian response and CPD priorities
Strengthened internal understanding of systems‑based WASH in fragile contexts
objectives:
• Strengthen integration between emergency and longer‑term WASH programming
  • Support transition from short‑term emergency service delivery to sustainable WASH systems
  • Improve technical design of WASH interventions in fragile and protracted crisis settings
  • Reduce recurrent emergency dependencies while safeguarding life‑saving outcomes
  • Align humanitarian WASH responses with CPD sustainability and resilience goals
  • Support WASH‑for‑Peace outcomes by promoting equitable, sustainable, and systems‑based WASH services in conflict‑affected settings, including Taiz

shortDescription: Participation of the Reference Group for the ¨Summative and formative evaluation of the out-of-school project implemented by UNICEF Venezuela¨
description:
The Education Specialist supporting the Evaluation Reference Group plays a technical advisory role throughout all phases of the evaluation, with a particular focus on educational quality, pedagogical relevance, and the coherence of the evaluative analysis of the Learning Recovery Programme for Out-of-School Children and Adolescents.
The primary responsibility of the Education Specialist is to provide specialized expertise in education, learning recovery, and educational pathways for out-of-school children and adolescents, ensuring that the evaluation:
• It is grounded in relevant pedagogical, policy, and programmatic frameworks.
• Adequately reflects the national and regional education context.
• Produces technically sound findings, conclusions, and recommendations that are relevant and actionable for decision-making.
The Education Specialist participates as an active member of the Evaluation Reference Group, contributing to the review and discussion of key consultancy deliverables (inception report, draft evaluation reports, and recommendations), engaging in technical meetings, and supporting the interpretation of results from an education-sector perspective.
The time commitment for this support is estimated at approximately two (2) working days across all stages of the evaluation.
objectives:
The participation of the Education Specialist aims to:

  1. Strengthen the technical quality of the evaluation by contributing specialized knowledge in education, learning recovery, and services for out-of-school children and adolescents.
  2. Contribute to the evaluation design and methodology, ensuring that the evaluative approach, questions, and tools are appropriate for assessing educational processes and learning outcomes in contexts of school exclusion.
  3. Provide substantive technical input during the review of evaluation products, ensuring that: analyses accurately reflect the complexity of the education sector, findings are correctly interpreted from a pedagogical perspective, and conclusions and recommendations are clear, feasible, and aligned with relevant education policies and frameworks.
  4. Support the utility and use of the evaluation, helping to ensure that results are relevant for programmatic and strategic decision-making by UNICEF and its partners.
  5. Facilitate alignment between the evaluation and the education sector, representing education-related priorities, perspectives, and information needs within the evaluation process.

shortDescription: COE Digital Expert Support for GCRI Roadmap Phase: Application Review, Transition Decisions & System Rationalization
description:
The Global Cyber Resiliency Initiative (GCRI) has completed the Assessment Phase, identifying 1,900+ digital systems across country offices, including T4D initiatives, fundraising platforms, and custom operational systems.

Assessment results reveal critical issues requiring expert evaluation during the Roadmap Phase, such as:

Fragmented system landscape; many systems built outside governance pathways.
High‑risk systems lacking maintenance contracts, proper hosting, authentication, or classification.
Need for programmatic validation to determine whether a system should be updated, transitioned, or decommissioned.

UNICEF lacks sufficient specialized digital expertise—particularly in product viability, architectural fitness, modernisation pathways, and field‑programme relevance—to ensure high‑quality decisions in the Roadmap Phase.

description: Technical Assistance for a National Community Health Strategy.Guinea-Bissau faces persistent political instability, weak institutions, limited basic services, and widespread poverty, contributing to some of the highest maternal and child mortality rates in West and Central Africa. Around 3,000 community health workers play a critical role in delivering essential health and nutrition services to vulnerable mothers and children. During the four-year period, 22,388 educators (95% of the total number) in public and private ECE institutions were empowered through a comprehensive capacity-building programme (blended training, mentoring, communities of practice) aimed at strengthening competencies for a new, high-quality, inclusive pedagogy, and more than 235,000 children benefited from their enhanced competencies. shortDescription: High-level advocacy and legal review to safeguard child rights, including draft law analysis and standards on minimum age of criminal responsibility.
description:
6. Child Rights Advocacy: Safeguarding Legal Standards and Policy Commitments for Adolescents

Technical support is required to provide high-level advocacy and legal review to safeguard child rights amid policy backsliding risks. This includes reviewing draft laws and policy proposals, preparing advocacy briefs, and providing technical advice on international standards related to minimum age of criminal responsibility and adolescent rights. Assistance will also involve developing evidence-based arguments, troubleshooting legislative gaps, and supporting UNICEF’s engagement with government and civil society to prevent harmful measures such as lowering the age of criminal responsibility or creating isolated facilities for adolescents. These targeted inputs will sustain ongoing advocacy and protect child rights commitments.
objectives: Curated collection of reviewed legal and policy documents with integrated technical feedback, supplemented by advocacy briefs and tailored talking points for high-level engagement with government and key stakeholders. These deliverables will reinforce UNICEF’s efforts to safeguard against harmful legislative changes and ensure alignment with international child rights standards.

shortDescription: Evaluate and renew national strategies to end child marriage through evidence-based, system-level reform
description: UNICEF Madagascar is requesting technical assistance to support the evaluation of the National Strategy on Ending Child Marriage (2017–2024). The implementation of the strategy faced a number of challenges, making a thorough evaluation essential before the development of a new strategy. During this period, the prevalence of girls aged 20–24 who were married before the age of 18 increased from 39% in 2018 to 42% in 2025, underscoring the need for sustained and strengthened national action. This includes continued multisectoral engagement and, based on the findings of the evaluation, the development of a new national strategy, with the mobilisation of key partners, including UNFPA.

shortDescription: Operationalize government-led programmes to prevent violence against girls, boys, and women using trauma-informed approaches
description:
TA to key stakeholders (health, education, social protection, justice) to develop, implement and monitor behaviorally and trauma-informed strategies and support interventions and awareness campaigns in ending all forms of violence against girls, boys and women (VAGBW) that focus on preventing physical, emotional, and sexual abuse by promoting safe environments at home, in schools, and online.
Kosovo currently lacks behaviorally informed and trauma informed strategies and operational tools for preventing VABGW at home, in schools and online. Despite the high prevalence of VAGBW, institutions across sectors (education, health, social welfare, justice, municipalities) have limited capacities to design, implement and monitor such approaches.
Technical Assistance is required to: 
1. Support the development of a multi-sectoral behaviorally and trauma informed VAGBW prevention Strategy.
2. Create implementation guidance, minimum standards, framework and monitoring tools. 
3. Strengthen institutional capacities to apply, scale and sustain these approaches across sectors in routine practice.
objectives:
Multi-sectoral behaviorally and trauma informed VAGBW prevention strategy developed.
Implementation toolkit: guidance, planning templates, monitoring framework developed and endorsed by the Key stakeholders (health, education, social protection, justice).
Cross-sectoral capacity-building package for institutionalizing these approaches are in place and integrated across sectors, promoting safe environments in homes, schools, and online.

The requested technical assistance will provide dedicated expertise to design, strengthen, and deliver the following specific outputs:

With Thailand/Myanmar Country Office colleagues, EAPRO public partnerships/Emergency teams (which will be transitioned to APRO from July 1st) and relevant CoE colleagues will be preparing a concept note together. Internally, within CoE, Yushi Yamada (WASH Officer-GPD-WASH) will kindly support the concept note development process and engagement and communication with the Embassy of Japan in Thailand, as one of CN's priorities will be on WASH and given the institutional knowledge and connections that CoE WASH Officer has been having with the Embassy. shortDescription: A four-day training on cash-based assistance in emergencies will be facilitated by COE Economic and Social Policy
description: A four-day training on cash-based assistance in emergencies will be facilitated by COE Economic and Social Policy. The training supports the introduction, scale-up, and institutionalization of cash-based assistance through national systems for emergency response. It targets mid- to senior-level officials from key ministries, including social protection, disaster risk management, finance, and local government, as well as relevant parastatal bodies at national and sub-national levels. The workshop will build a shared understanding of how and why to operationalize cash assistance, identify system gaps and opportunities, clarify partner contributions, and define priority next steps, laying a foundation for collaboration and faster disaster responses
objectives: Participants will have a shared understanding of i) why and how to operationalize cash-based assistance in response to disasters, ii) the gaps and opportunities for reinforcing national systems, iii) the contributions that key development partners can make to national system strengthening, and iv) the priority next steps to be taken. In doing so, the workshop will help lay a solid foundation for sustained collaboration and faster progress toward more effective and timely responses to future disasters.

shortDescription: Evaluate and renew national strategies to end child marriage through evidence-based, system-level reform
description:
Technical support for a multisectoral evaluation of the National Strategy to End Child Marriage (2017–2024), and in a second phase, support for the development of a new national strategy, elevating attention and action on a persisting issue requiring attention. (Policy Reform and Programme Design)
UNICEF Madagascar is requesting technical assistance to support the evaluation of the National Strategy on Ending Child Marriage (2017–2024). The implementation of the strategy faced a number of challenges, making a thorough evaluation essential before the development of a new strategy. During this period, the prevalence of girls aged 20–24 who were married before the age of 18 increased from 39% in 2018 to 42% in 2025, underscoring the need for sustained and strengthened national action. This includes continued multisectoral engagement and, based on the findings of the evaluation, the development of a new national strategy, with the mobilisation of key partners, including UNFPA.
objectives: Evaluation of the National Strategy on Ending Child Marriage in Madagascar (2017–2024) completed, with a new national strategy under development  (unlikely to be finalised within the same year).

shortDescription: Request to reinstate the Learning Passport (LP) platform in Mozambique, following its shutdown last November due to inactivity.
description:
UNICEF Mozambique has reassessed the situation and successfully re-engaged the Ministry of Education, renewing interest in leveraging technology to transform the education system. The urgency is clear: Mozambique faces significant challenges in ensuring learning continuity. Over two million children remain out of school, dropout rates are high and learning outcomes for those enrolled are alarmingly low. The education system is overstretched and underfunded, and the outlook is further complicated by rapid population growth, economic stagnation, ongoing conflict, and the impacts of climate change.

To reverse this downward trend, a bold transformation of the education sector is needed—one that harnesses the power of technology to expand access, improve quality, and build resilience. In close coordination with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF Mozambique is committed to reviving the Learning Passport with a clear and strategic vision and building on lessons learned from previous efforts:

• To deliver curriculum-aligned content to children both in and out of school
• To build foundational and 21st-century skills
• To strengthen teacher capacity through digital professional development modules
objectives: https://moz.learningpassport.org is up and running

At present, the TLCO has limited in-house expertise on climate-smart infrastructure. Only one engineering consultant is currently supporting the design and monitoring of the solarization component, which creates capacity constraints in developing additional funding proposals and accessing technical guidance on climate-resilient infrastructure.

For long-term interventions in this area, it will be important to have clear guidance and advisory support on design standards, costing, and operation and maintenance (O&M), to enable the CO to effectively plan, implement, and scale up climate-resilient infrastructure interventions.

shortDescription: Establish a national, child-centred DRM policy embedding resilience, early warning, and climate adaptation across sectors.
description:
Module A — DRM Policy co-design & consultation (≈ 10–12 weeks) 

What CoE does: Provide policy drafting support (structure, content, inter-ministerial roles) and facilitate a concise consultative process at national and zoba levels; prepare an operationalization plan (governance, SOPs, early warning, preparedness drills, financing hooks). 

What it strengthens: A child-centred DRM Policy, validated and ready for adoption, with a clear action plan and role handshakes. 

Standards/tools: UNICEF CEED/DRR guidance; consultation playbook; operational plan templates. 

Module B — Light vulnerability profiling (2–3 zobas) 

What CoE does: Apply a rapid, indicator-based profile (hazard exposure, WASH/health/nutrition access, school resilience, protection risks); map existing assets (solar water systems, catchments, early warning practices). 

What it strengthens: Practical evidence to prioritize resilience investments and preparedness routines. 

Standards/tools: Rapid profiling toolkit; simple geotag forms; child risk lens (LNOB/HRBA). 

Module C — Programme integration: shock-resilience & climate adaptation 

What CoE does: Run short design clinics with WASH/Health/Nutrition/Education/Child Protection to embed resilience add-ons (e.g., climate-resilient WASH O&M, school safety/continuity, nutrition continuity, protection case-management contingencies). 

What it strengthens: Realistic resilience features inside ongoing activities; documented add-ons and quick wins. 

Standards/tools: Resilience add-on menu; preparedness SOPs; continuity checklists. 

Module D — Early warning & preparedness routines (lite) 

What CoE does: Set up simple early warning triggers and action protocols in pilot zobas; support quarterly preparedness drills; create a one-page dashboard for PMT/CMT. 

What it strengthens: Predictable preparedness and faster response; leadership visibility on risk status. 

Standards/tools: EW trigger table; drill playbook; dashboard template.
objectives:
Q1 2026 

- Inception: scope, governance (lead ministry + MoLWE/MoH/MoE + UNICEF), data inventory. 

- DRM Policy skeleton + consultation plan (national & zoba). 

- Light vulnerability profiling design + site selection. 

Q2 2026 

- Consultations conducted; DRM Policy (draft) completed. 

- Vulnerability profiling implemented in 2–3 zobas; profiles (draft) produced. 

- Design clinics: sector resilience add-ons documented; EW trigger table drafted. 

Q3 2026 

- DRM Policy validated; Operational Plan agreed (inter-ministerial). 

- EW/Preparedness routines piloted; first drills completed; dashboard v1 shared. 

- Zoba profiles (final) endorsed; quick win investments listed. 

Q4 2026 

- Adoption package prepared; handover of SOPs/templates; mentoring log. 

- Replication roadmap agreed with ministries; TA Close-out Note.

Under the climate action and youth flagship area, the new programme of cooperation aims to significantly increase the number of children and young people equipped with climate adaptation and DRR knowledge and skills, while promoting sustainable “green” behaviours. These efforts are fully aligned with the country’s 2030 Agenda commitments, the National Climate Change Strategy, the National Action Plan for Realization of Children’s Rights (2023-2028), and the NDC. A key component is the expansion of the national “Green School” initiative — jointly launched with the Ministry of Education in 2025 — with plans to reach 500 schools by 2030. 1. Child Protection System Strengthening, continue strengthening the child protection system through policy advocacy and implementation, and by supporting planning, budgeting, and monitoring—particularly at the subnational level—alongside sustained investment in the social service workforce including in humanitarian setting.
2.  Online Child Protection, as Indonesia advances online child protection, support from the COE is critical to share good practices on in applying the "whole society approach" including engaging electronic system providers to promote “safety by design” and to support the development of monitoring platforms for self-assessment and compliance.

shortDescription: The programme requires periodic technical support to inform design and sustain implementation

For social workforce strengthening and children's care reform, support is needed to participate in consultations, organize study tours, and review documents. On the integration of child protection and social policy, inputs are required to build the case management system for Cash++. For MRM/CAAC, short-term assistance is needed to organize and deliver a training-of-trainers on the MRM. Further technical support might be required to strengthen responses for children on the move. This would include guidance for the development of standardized cross-border case management mechanisms, ensuring coherent procedures.
objectives: The output expected includes mainly: Validated Child Protection coordination survey results and a finalized action plan, along with a technically reviewed annual report; Documented technical inputs from consultations, including reviewed materials supporting social workforce strengthening and care reform, in addition to enhanced capacity through the organization of study tours; Updated and technically-supported materials contributing to the development of the Cash++ case management system; An established pool of trainers on MRM, ensuring practical, day-to-day tools and documents are produced and maintained to support ongoing programme implementation. The technical support is also expected to result in clear guidance and draft tools for strengthening responses for children on the move, including initial standardized procedures and templates for cross-border case management, developed with support from the CoEs.

This includes reviewing implementation guidelines and training materials, providing targeted inputs to strengthen coordination mechanisms, and troubleshooting operational challenges during rollout. Assistance will also involve technical review of monitoring tools, periodic feedback on progress reports, and guidance on integrating VAC prevention into existing child protection and education platforms. These practical, day-to-day interventions will ensure timely implementation and alignment with national standards and UNICEF’s child protection priorities.

shortDescription: Transform juvenile justice systems to prioritize prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation through child-sensitive, rights-based approaches
description:
2.Juvenile Justice System Reform: Strengthening Prevention, Diversion, and Rehabilitation for Children in Conflict with the Law

This initiative aims to transform the juvenile justice system into a child-sensitive, rights-based framework that prioritizes prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation over punitive measures. The strategic purpose is to reduce the criminalization of children and ensure compliance with international standards, while addressing root causes of offending behavior. The intended system-level change is the institutionalization of integrated mechanisms—policy, protocols, and services—that enable early intervention, community-based alternatives, and structured rehabilitation programs. This reform will strengthen coordination among justice, social welfare, and education sectors, ensuring sustainable, scalable solutions that protect children’s rights and promote reintegration into society.
Technical assistance is required to re-design and institutionalize a child-sensitive juvenile justice framework that embeds prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation as core principles. This support will help develop national standards, operational guidelines, and inter-agency coordination mechanisms to replace punitive approaches with restorative practices. It will also guide the creation of structured diversion programs, community-based rehabilitation services, and capacity-building plans for justice and social welfare actors. By integrating these reforms into policy and practice, the assistance will deliver a sustainable system that protects children’s rights, reduces recidivism, and strengthens cross-sector collaboration for holistic child protection.
objectives: An endorsed national juvenile justice reform framework signed by the Government, including agreed standards for prevention, diversion, and rehabilitation, and an operational roadmap for implementation. This milestone will confirm institutional commitment and provide a structured plan for scaling child-sensitive justice practices nationwide.

shortDescription: Scale justice for children from pilot initiatives to a national system
description:
Scaling up justice for children – from pilot to national model
UNICEF is currently implementing an integrated service package for justice for children in one major urban area (Kandy). By end-Q1 2026, the first six months of implementation of this pilot will provide operational evidence to assess functionality, gaps, and system-readiness for expansion. UNICEF will need to assess and use that evidence to propose a cost-efficient pathway for sustainable scale-up nationwide. This will likely include adjusting institutional responsibilities, refining the model based on early lessons, and developing a scalable financing and workforce approach. The specifics—appropriate sequencing, cost implications, and political feasibility—will become clearer once early performance data and feedback is analysed with UNICEF’s aim being to ensure that a realistic, evidence-based scale-up plan is on the table for government consideration by Q2/Q3 to feed into the preparation of the 2027 budget planning process.
objectives:
Pilot performance and system-readiness assessment. An evidence-based assessment of the first six months of implementation, identifying what works, what needs adjustment, and the system implications for scale-up.
Costed national scale-up pathway for justice for children. A phased, financially and institutionally feasible plan for national expansion, designed to feed directly into 2027 budget and policy processes

shortDescription: Technical assistance to strengthen climate‑resilient and standards‑compliant WASH in institutions, with a focus on World Bank‑aligned WASH in health facilities
description:
This technical assistance will provide specialized support to strengthen the technical quality, climate resilience, and sustainability of WASH services in institutions, with a primary focus on health facilities and targeted support to schools and learning environments where relevant. The TA will emphasize system functionality, reliability, and long‑term operation and maintenance, rather than standalone infrastructure delivery.
For health facilities, the assistance will focus on improving water supply reliability, sanitation and wastewater management, hygiene infrastructure, and waste management systems, ensuring alignment with international infection prevention and control (IPC) standards and World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS). Particular attention will be given to climate‑resilient design, including water source resilience, backup systems, and adaptation to climate risks such as droughts and floods.
The TA will support technical design review, development of practical guidance and standards, and strengthening of operation and maintenance (O&M) arrangements for institutional WASH. This support will help reduce implementation and compliance risks, particularly in the context of World Bank‑financed health sector operations, while improving sustainability and service continuity in fragile and climate‑stressed environments.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables

Technical guidance and review inputs for WASH in health facilities and schools
Climate‑resilient design and O&M recommendations for institutional WASH systems
Strengthened alignment with IPC standards and World Bank ESS requirements
Improved technical capacity of staff and partners on institutional WASH quality assurance
objectives:
• Improve technical quality and sustainability of WASH services in health facilities and schools
  • Strengthen climate‑resilient design and functionality of institutional WASH systems
  • Support compliance with international IPC standards and World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS) for WASH in health facilities
  • Reduce operational, environmental, and reputational risks associated with institutional WASH investments
  • Strengthen UNICEF and partner capacity to design, implement, and supervise high‑quality WASH in institutions under the CPD

shortDescription: WASH Information Management, GIS & Digital Monitoring Systems
description:
This technical assistance will support UNICEF Yemen to strengthen WASH information management systems, including the use of GIS, digital monitoring tools, and integrated data platforms to support evidence‑based planning, programme monitoring, and decision‑making. The TA will focus on improving data quality, interoperability, and practical use of WASH data across humanitarian and development programming.
Support will include technical guidance on GIS‑based mapping of WASH infrastructure and services, development or refinement of digital monitoring frameworks, and integration of WASH data with climate risk, water resources, and health indicators where feasible. The assistance will also help strengthen capacity for routine data analysis, visualization, and use at national and sub‑national levels, ensuring that digital tools support programme quality, accountability, and adaptive management rather than parallel reporting systems.

Expected Outputs / Deliverables

GIS and digital monitoring guidance adapted to Yemen WASH context
Improved WASH data frameworks and visualization tools
Strengthened capacity of staff and partners on WASH information management
Better integration of WASH data into planning and reporting processes
objectives:
• Strengthen WASH information management systems to support CPD implementation
  • Improve use of GIS and spatial analysis for WASH planning and targeting
  • Enhance digital monitoring and reporting of WASH services and system functionality
  • Support evidence‑based decision‑making across humanitarian and development WASH programming
  • Improve data availability for climate resilience, cholera prevention, and systems strengthening

shortDescription: We request technical support to develop a new Country Programme Document (CPD) with a strong social policy focus
description:
We request technical support to develop a new Country Programme Document (CPD) with a strong social policy focus. The support is needed to help shape the overall policy framework and ensure the CPD is grounded in evidence-based social policy analysis.

In particular, we require technical assistance to design a clear and actionable strategy to strengthen public financing for children. This should include analysis of current financing gaps, policy and budgetary constraints, and options to improve the adequacy, efficiency, and equity of public spending for children.

The technical support will contribute to aligning the CPD with national priorities, strengthening its policy coherence, and ensuring that proposed interventions are feasible, sustainable, and impactful.
objectives:
A revised CPD with a strong and coherent social policy framework, grounded in evidence and aligned with national development priorities.

A clear, costed strategy to strengthen public financing for children, including practical policy options to improve the adequacy, efficiency, and equity of public spending.

Improved analysis of fiscal space, budget processes, and financing bottlenecks affecting investments in children.

Strengthened capacity of relevant stakeholders to engage in social policy dialogue and advocate for increased and more effective public financing for children.

Actionable recommendations to support implementation, monitoring, and sustainability of social policy and financing reforms within the CPD period.

shortDescription: Participation on the Reference Group for the ¨Summative and formative evaluation of the out-of-school project implemented by UNICEF Venezuela¨
description:
The Education Specialist supporting the Evaluation Reference Group plays a technical advisory role throughout all phases of the evaluation, with a particular focus on educational quality, pedagogical relevance, and the coherence of the evaluative analysis of the Learning Recovery Programme for Out-of-School Children and Adolescents.

The primary responsibility of the Education Specialist is to provide specialized expertise in education, learning recovery, and educational pathways for out-of-school children and adolescents, ensuring that the evaluation:

• It is grounded in relevant pedagogical, policy, and programmatic frameworks.

• Adequately reflects the national and regional education context.

• Produces technically sound findings, conclusions, and recommendations that are relevant and actionable for decision-making.

The Education Specialist participates as an active member of the Evaluation Reference Group, contributing to the review and discussion of key consultancy deliverables (inception report, draft evaluation reports, and recommendations), engaging in technical meetings, and supporting the interpretation of results from an education-sector perspective.
The time commitment for this support is estimated at approximately two (2) working days across all stages of the evaluation.
objectives:
The participation of the Education Specialist aims to:

Strengthen the technical quality of the evaluation by contributing specialized knowledge in education, learning recovery, and services for out-of-school children and adolescents.
Contribute to the evaluation design and methodology, ensuring that the evaluative approach, questions, and tools are appropriate for assessing educational processes and learning outcomes in contexts of school exclusion.

Provide substantive technical input during the review of evaluation products, ensuring that: analyses accurately reflect the complexity of the education sector, findings are correctly interpreted from a pedagogical perspective, and conclusions and recommendations are clear, feasible, and aligned with relevant education policies and frameworks.

Support the utility and use of the evaluation, helping to ensure that results are relevant for programmatic and strategic decision-making by UNICEF and its partners.

Facilitate alignment between the evaluation and the education sector, representing education-related priorities, perspectives, and information needs within the evaluation process.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description: Malawi’s primary health care system faces persistent financing challenges, with declining prioritization of immunisation and essential PHC services threatening service continuity and sustainability. Despite the Government’s commitment to Universal Health Coverage, budget allocations and execution for immunisation remain constrained by competing fiscal pressures, foreign exchange volatility, and limited medium-term expenditure planning. Strengthening domestic financing for PHC is critical to safeguard essential services and ensure sustainable vaccine delivery in line with HSSP III and the Lusaka Agenda.To address these challenges, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to strengthen domestic financing for PHC, with a focus on reversing the declining prioritization of immunisation financing. The support will build on ongoing CO budget analysis work, translating fiscal evidence into actionable analytics and policy tools to influence Government of Malawi, Ministry of Health, and Treasury investment decisions. It will consolidate and deepen current PHC and immunisation financing analyses through a rapid diagnostic integrating budget trends, execution performance, and immunisation sustainability modelling. The TA will generate forward-looking scenarios for vaccine co-financing under varying macroeconomic conditions, assess delivery cost bottlenecks and value-for-money opportunities, and identify practical efficiency and reprioritization levers. Additionally, it will support the development of a budget protection framework for vaccines and essential PHC services, including earmarking and contingency financing options, medium-term expenditure projections, and concrete policy measures to strengthen immunisation prioritization within MoH budgets and the national Medium-Term Expenditure Framework.
objectives: ∙A comprehensive PHC and immunisation financing diagnostic, integrating budget trends, execution performance, and sustainability modelling, aligned with HSSP III and the Lusaka Agenda.∙Forward-looking scenarios for vaccine co-financing under different macroeconomic conditions, including fiscal risk analysis, delivery cost bottlenecks, and value-for-money opportunities.∙A practical budget protection and prioritization framework for vaccines and essential PHC services, with policy recommendations, medium-term expenditure projections, and advocacy tools for Ministry of Health, Treasury, and Cabinet decision-making

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description:
Zimbabwe is implementing the HPV Plus initiative under its National HPV Revitalization Strategy, approved in February 2025, which aims to raise HPV vaccination coverage to 90% by 2030. The strategy aligns with WHO guidance by introducing a differentiated schedule for adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV), who require two doses instead of the single dose given to the general population.
Despite this progress, major gaps persist in reaching ALHIV, who face a higher risk of persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer. Coverage remains particularly low among out‑of‑school adolescents and those from marginalized groups. Weak integration between HIV care services and HPV vaccination programs leads to missed opportunities to identify ALHIV and ensure completion of the two‑dose schedule. In addition, many healthcare providers lack sufficient training to deliver differentiated HPV services and tailored counselling. These challenges are further compounded by poorly integrated HIV and HPV data systems, limiting effective tracking of vaccination status and follow‑up for second doses. To operationalize the HPV Plus initiative for adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV), Zimbabwe requires targeted technical assistance to strengthen differentiated HPV vaccination delivery. Priority needs include developing standardized operational guidance and user‑friendly job aids to support implementation of the two‑dose schedule, and identifying effective service delivery platforms informed by best practices from countries with successful ALHIV HPV vaccination programs.
objectives: Increased proportion of ALHIV receiving complete and timely 2‑dose HPV vaccination, contributing to the national target of 90% coverage.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description:
This technical assistance will provide strategic and technical support to the UNICEF CO in Kyrgyzstan and national stakeholders to enable the timely and high quality development of the country’s Gavi 6.0 proposal. The assistance will focus on clarifying the strategic direction, priorities, and scope of the forthcoming application, ensuring strong alignment with national immunization goals, health sector strategies, and Gavi 6.0 strategic principles.
The assistance will facilitate early and meaningful alignment between national immunization priorities, lessons learned from ongoing and past Gavi supported interventions, and emerging Gavi 6.0 requirements. Through structured consultations and technical inputs, the in-person mission in April 2026 will support the development of a high level conceptual framework and outline that positions the Gavi application as a coherent, holistic, and forward looking investment package.
In parallel, the mission in April will help strengthen internal CO capacity through targeted technical briefings and knowledge transfer on immunization and the Gavi portfolio. Particular emphasis will be placed on supporting the induction and strategic orientation of the new Chief of Health (TA), ensuring continuity of technical leadership and informed decision making throughout the Gavi 6.0 preparation process.
Overall, the technical assistance will enhance strategic coherence, technical quality, and institutional readiness, laying a strong foundation for a competitive and impactful Gavi 6.0 country proposal submitted by December 2026.
objectives:
1.Strategic direction and prioritization for the Gavi 6.0 application established
Clear strategic direction, priorities, and scope for the Gavi 6.0 application are articulated, informed by national policy frameworks, programmatic evidence, equity considerations, and future system needs.
2.Early strategic alignment achieved btw national priorities and Gavi 6.0 Framework
Early and sustained alignment is facilitated btw national immunization strategies, lessons learned from current and past Gavi grants, and Gavi 6.0 principles, ensuring coherence, continuity, and value for money.
3.High level conceptual framework for the Gavi 6.0 application developed in cooperation with MoH and WHO
A high-level conceptual framework and draft outline for a holistic and integrated Gavi 6.0 country proposal is developed, articulating strategic objectives, investment priorities, and anticipated results across immunization and health systems.
4.Gavi 6.0 Country Proposal developed and submitted (by December 2026)
A comprehensive, high quality Gavi 6.0 country proposal is developed and formally submitted, aligned with national immunization priorities, health system strengthening objectives, and Gavi 6.0 strategic directions.
5.Strengthened technical capacity and institutional knowledge within the CO
Targeted technical briefings and structured knowledge transfer are delivered to the CO, including dedicated support for the induction of the new Chief of Health (TA), strengthening institutional understanding of immunization programming.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description: Malawi continues to face  challenges related to zero-dose and missed children. Reaching zero-dose children and missed children requires an integrated primary health care (PHC) approach that address gender-related barriers, social norms, and structural barriers, while building resilient and sustained demand for immunisation services. Improved health outcomes depend on empowered communities and strengthened social accountability mechanisms that actively engage communities in participatory planning, implementation, and monitoring of health services. Building and sustaining trust in immunisation services is therefore essential and requires timely, coordinated, and evidence-based responses to community voices, concerns and satisfaction. Malawi Country Office has been collecting community feedback, rumours, and misinformation through multiple channels—both online (e.g. U-Report, media monitoring) and offline (surveys, rapid qualitative assessments, and field monitoring) but these data remain fragmented. Information is stored across different platforms and its lacks  national feedback system which consolidate, analyse, and act on community insights.There is a critical need to establish one  community feedback and response mechanism that integrates data from all existing platforms. This system will be able to do real-time analysis, coordinated response planning, and systematic use of community feedback to inform programme adjustments and policy decisions. This mechanism will support evidence-based decision-making, improve responsiveness  to community concerns and rumours, and ultimately strengthen demand for immunisation and other essential health services.
objectives: Review of existing feedback mechanism (tools, guidance including mechanism) to understand patient satisfaction, rumors and misinformation identification including gap analysisDesign of the feedback mechanism and advocacy strategy to for inclusion within existing government system. Capacity development package (tools, guidance and resource materials) for relevant stakeholders on identification of rumors, misinformation, data collection tools and data entry and analysis.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description:
There is growing recognition within Viet Nam’s Ministry of Health (MOH) and other line ministries of the need for more comprehensive, system-oriented SBC strategies. However, institutional capacity for SBC research, design, implementation, and monitoring remains limited. With increasing digital connectivity, there is also a need to better integrate behavioral insights and digital engagement to enhance inclusion, equity, and sustainability.
Strengthening SBC across sectors will support more effective health and social interventions, greater community participation, and sustainable behavior change at scale.
To address this, UNICEF Viet Nam, in collaboration with MOH, is conducting a rapid organizational and capacity assessment of SBC programmes, with a focus on immunization. The assessment will identify key barriers to scale and existing capacities within the health system.
Based on the findings, UNICEF will support the development of an SBC curriculum to strengthen MOH staff capacity in planning, budgeting, managing, and monitoring SBC programmes.
UNICEF Viet Nam is seeking TA support to provide technical review, inputs, and guidance to ensure the quality of both the assessment and the curriculum development.
objectives:
By June 2026, organizational barriers to the large-scale delivery of SBC, as well as existing competencies and capacities within the health system, are identified through an SBC capacity assessment.
By December 2026, the capacity of health staff to plan, budget, manage, and monitor SBC strategies and programmes is strengthened through the development and piloting of an SBC curriculum.

objectives: To scale up the prototypes tested across Pakistan (from service delivery adaptations, infrastructure improvements, and community engagement models), there is need for dedicated technical coordination support. The real world testing of eight priority prototypes across more than 16 districts generated substantial evidence on what works in low performing and marginalized settings (e.g., redesigned clinic experiences, mobile immunization with community guides, culturally competent navigators, child friendly clinics, community champion networks). Several of these prototypes require concrete changes to infrastructure, including signage, caregiver flow, child friendly spaces, and minor structural redesigns. UNICEF wants to take the opportunity of the ongoing refurbishment of 2,000 health facilities to establish fully functional EPI service points to implement some of these recommendations linked to infrastructure. It requires systematic coordination to ensure that service delivery redesigns, infrastructural improvements, and community engagement models are tailored to specific provincial, district, or selected UC contexts. The country team is engaged in many other priority activities, and do not want to miss the opportunity to implement innovative approaches that may bring positive changes to the program, in reaching children at the last mile to improve coverage.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description: Malawi’s community health workforce including HSAs, CHNs, and CHVs forms the backbone of primary health care delivery, particularly at the community level. Despite their critical role, the workforce faces fragmented career pathways, limited progression opportunities, and inconsistent integration into formal health structures. Strengthening the professionalisation of this cadre is essential to improve motivation, retention, and quality of service delivery, in line with HSSP III, the National Community Health Framework, and broader HRH reforms.To address these gaps, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to professionalise the community health workforce, with a primary focus on designing clear career progression pathways. The support will define competency standards, accreditation, and progression for all community cadres, integrate them into formal PHC structures with appropriate supervision and retention mechanisms, ensure alignment with district operational plans and national HRH systems, and provide guidance for institutionalisation and sustainable workforce management to strengthen PHC delivery and advance Universal Health Coverage.
objectives: ∙A professionalisation framework for community health cadres, including clear career progression pathways, competency standards, accreditation mechanisms, and integration into formal PHC structures with supervision and retention strategies.∙Practical guidance for institutionalisation and sustainable workforce management, aligned with district operational plans and national HRH systems, to strengthen PHC delivery and advance Universal Health Coverage.

shortDescription: Please insert a short description with not more than 160 characters, including spaces
description: Malawi’s primary health care system is increasingly exposed to multiple emergency hazards, including climate shocks, disease outbreaks, and other public health threats, which threaten service continuity and resilience. Despite progress in PHC coverage, emergency events can rapidly disrupt essential services, particularly for vulnerable populations. Strengthening system resilience and maintaining or increasing PHC intervention coverage requires strategic approaches that integrate preparedness, adaptive service delivery, and coordinated response mechanisms, in line with HSSP III and broader health sector reforms.To address these challenges, UNICEF Malawi requests technical assistance to support the strategic design and implementation of PHC interventions that maintain and expand coverage while enhancing system resilience. The support will focus on adaptive service delivery models, strategic prepositioning of essential supplies and resources, and the development of expanded multi-stakeholder partnerships to ensure continuity of services during emergencies. The TA will provide guidance on operationalising emergency preparedness and response plans within routine PHC delivery, identifying system bottlenecks, optimizing resource allocation, and integrating lessons from previous hazard responses to strengthen both short-term emergency response and long-term system resilience.Expected outputs include a strategic framework for resilient PHC delivery under emergency conditions, operational guidance for adaptive service delivery, prepositioning plans for essential supplies, and partnership strategies to support sustainable emergency response and continuity of essential PHC services.
objectives: ∙A strategic framework and operational guidance for resilient PHC delivery, including adaptive service delivery models, prepositioning of essential supplies, and integration of emergency preparedness and response into routine PHC services.∙Partnership strategies and actionable tools to support multi-stakeholder coordination, optimize resource allocation, and maintain or expand PHC coverage during emergencies.

shortDescription: Shift Eritrea’s food systems from production-focused approaches to nutrition outcomes through integrated value chains, schools, food safety, and SBC
description:
Module A — Rapid food systems mapping & priority entry points (≈ 8 weeks) 

What CoE does: Produce a concise map of nutrition-sensitive value chains (e.g., cereals/legumes, dairy) and school-based entry points (gardens/menus), with a baseline of risks and simple indicators. Identify quick wins in food safety and hygiene practices across small processors/school kitchens; map governance and cross-ministry roles (MoA/MoH/MoE/MLWE). 

What it strengthens: Shared picture of “where to start” linking production to nutrition outcomes; early list of feasible pilots; clarity on roles and decision points. 

Standards/tools: UNICEF food systems/nutrition guidance; simple value-chain and risk screening templates; school nutrition checklist. 

Module B — Complementary foods mini-pilot (DMK+) & micro-processing support 

What CoE does: Co-design a small DMK+ complementary food mini-pilot: product specifications, quality/batch SOPs, basic HACCP-inspired hygiene steps, packaging/labelling, and micro-processing coaching for 2–3 local producer units (or school kitchens). Develop simple QA tools and a child-feeding counselling card that links to the product. 

What it strengthens: Safe, acceptable complementary foods with clear quality steps; local capacity to produce and coach caregivers; documented micro-processing SOPs for replication. 

Standards/tools: UNICEF IYCF resources; QA/food safety lite templates; behaviour change job-aids. 

Module C — Food safety & fortification “lite”: SOPs and training 

What CoE does: Draft light SOPs for hygiene, storage, and fortification/processing suitable for small establishments and schools; run two short training cycles (virtual + in-country practical sessions) for MoH/MoA/MoE/MMR/MTI teams and local producers. Provide model procurement specs (e.g., packaging, basic test kits) and simple monitoring forms. 

What it strengthens: Practical, context-appropriate standards that reduce contamination and variability; entry-level capacity to monitor compliance. 

Standards/tools: Food safety checklists; school kitchen hygiene SOP; fortification basics; simple monitoring templates. 

Module D — Healthy diets SBC & school-based pilots (gardens/menus/peer clubs) 

What CoE does: Package an SBC toolkit (scripts/posters/mini-sessions) on diverse diets and safe food handling; set up 10–15 school garden/menu/peer clubs pilots with seasonally feasible crops and a simple menu planning sheet; define a light results log (attendance, menu diversity, hygiene practices). 

What it strengthens: Community and school behaviours for healthier diets; practical experience with school gardens and simple menu standards; early evidence for scale-up. 

Standards/tools: SBC toolkit; garden starter kit; menu diversity scorecard; hygiene reminders.
objectives:
Q1 2026 

- Inception: scope, governance (MoA/MoH/MoE/MLWE/MTI/MMR + UNICEF), data inventory. 

- Rapid mapping (draft): value chains, school entry points, risks, pilot shortlist. 

- DMK+ mini-pilot setup: equipment specs, product specs, QA/batch SOPs, training plan. 

Q2 2026 

- Food safety/fortification SOPs (v1) + training cycle #1 (virtual). 

- DMK+ micro-processing pilots start (2–3 units); QA tools distributed. 

- School pilots start (10–15 gardens/menus); SBC kit delivered; light results log activated. 

Q3 2026 

- Training cycle #2 (in-country practical); SOPs (v2) refined. 

- Pilot reviews: DMK+ and school pilots—quick wins and corrective notes. 

- Draft “Food Systems for Children” brief for hearings/UNSDCF dialogue. 

Q4 2026 

- Consolidation: Starter Pack finalized (templates, SOPs, SBC kit). 

- Handover: mentoring log; replication plan with ministries; TA Close-out Note.

shortDescription: Prevent post-cyclone nutrition and food security crises through anticipatory, child-focused action
description: UNICEF anticipates heightened food insecurity in Q2–Q3 2026 as the cumulative effects of Cyclone Ditwah, high food prices, and already elevated child malnutrition converge. Both wasting and stunting rates were concerning prior to the cyclone, and we expect additional shocks to push vulnerable households into deeper food stress. Our priority for 2026 is to position UNICEF to lead the development of a coherent package of short-term and medium-term interventions—ranging from targeted nutrition support and continuity of essential services to systems-level measures that strengthen surveillance, early warning, and household resilience. Sri Lanka will have limited fiscal space next year (and the CO will have limited funding) but the need for clear analysis, costed options, and strong advocacy remains urgent. UNICEF will need to identify feasible entry points and shaping an integrated proposal/clear advocacy that government and partners can get behind, rollout and budget for in subsequent years.
objectives:
Integrated child nutrition and food-security risk outlook (2026–27). A concise, evidence-based analysis identifying priority risks, population groups, and geographic hotspots, with clear scenario projections to inform government and partner decision-making.

Costed response and advocacy package for 2027 budget planning. A small set of realistic, costed intervention options—sequenced and prioritised under fiscal constraints—presented in a government-ready format to support policy decisions and advocacy.

shortDescription: Support development and review of climate rationales for Somaliland and Puntland.
description:
Development of a climate rationale is one of the key priorities under ASWA III.
The process is already underway in both states, with Somaliland having completed the climate risk analysis and solutions workshop to identify feasible measures to address the identified risks.
The climate rationales will support:
• Policy and planning processes
• Design and targeting of climate resilient WASH programmes
• Development of climate finance proposals, including for the Green Climate Fund
• Improved alignment between WASH and climate priorities, including Somalia’s updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and the National Adaptation Plan (NAP)

The required support includes technical review of the climate risk and solutions reports generated through these processes, as well as review of the final Climate Rationale products for Somaliland and Puntland.
objectives: To strengthen climate-resilient WASH planning, investment, and programming.

shortDescription: Support for WASH-focused conflict and peace analysis.
description:
WASH Conflict Analysis is a key priority under ASWA III.
The purpose of the WASH Conflict Analysis is to develop and implement a WASH focused Conflict and Peace Analysis (CPA) that integrates gender equality, disability, and social inclusion considerations, and to use the findings to strengthen the integration of conflict sensitivity and peacebuilding into WASH programming. The participatory conflict analysis will support identification and addressing of the root causes of WASH related conflict in Puntland and Somaliland, while targeted capacity development support will strengthen the capacity of UNICEF staff and sector partners.
The required support to the Somalia Country Office includes review of the WASH Conflict Analysis report and development of training materials to support capacity building of staff and partners for effective integration of the findings into conflict sensitive and peacebuilding focused WASH programming.
objectives: To integrate conflict-sensitive and peacebuilding approaches into WASH programming.

shortDescription: Technical assistance to the PCO in the review of the technical design and potential implementation oversight support for a solar WASH project
description:
Technical support – Phillipines Solar PV (Tawi-Tawi Project). PCO initially proceeded by engaging a solar PV consultant to provide technical oversight and ensure quality assurance across design, procurement, and installation phases. However, the CO encountered a key constraint ,limited availability of specialized PV expertise in the current market, particularly with experience in complex, remote, and fragile contexts such as Tawi-Tawi. This created delays and required them to rethink their approach as they still do not a PV consultant on board. To further address this, PCO adapted the structure of the engagement and split the institutional ToR into two phases:
1. Technical Assessment and System Design (current phase)
2. Supply, Installation, and Commissioning (implementation phase)
PCO now have SESCO engaged as the technical design firm, and Daniel’s team has been instrumental in supporting the technical review and strengthening the quality of this process.
Looking ahead, PCO are planning a project inception in June, which will bring together relevant BARMM line ministries, and the Languyan local government unit. This will be a critical milestone to align on the technical design, confirm roles and responsibilities, and ensure government ownership from the outset.

shortDescription: UNICEF Armenia Country Office is keen to engage in the expansion of innovative learning programmes under UNICEF’s new global education strategy, particularly it
description:
UNICEF Armenia Country Office's interest in exploring the opportunity to participate in the expansion of innovative learning programmes, announced as part of UNICEF's transformative global education strategy launched at Educa in Helsinki last week. I am particularly inspired by the Strategy's deliberate shifts toward putting teachers and learners at the center while prioritizing equity.
 
The Government of Armenia recognizes the critical importance of EdTech to transform education delivery. Active discussions are currently underway at the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sports (MoESCS) with relevant stakeholders regarding the role of EdTech and AI in education. While several pilot and innovative initiatives exist in both formal and informal education, a comprehensive framework and system-wide approach are currently missing—making this an opportune moment for UNICEF strategic intervention.
 
Armenia presents a unique opportunity for scaling innovative learning programmes due to the strong government commitment to digital transformation and presence of companies delivering innovative solutions. In 2024, the MoESCS adopted new state standards for Digital Literacy and Computer Science (DLCS), aiming to equip students with practical, future-ready programming skills, computational thinking, and digital literacy. To ensure effective implementation of these standards, UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministry and in partnership with the Foundation for Armenian Science and Technology (FAST), is supporting a pilot programme to capacitate DLCS teachers to deliver the new curriculum. We are simultaneously supporting the digitalization of teacher training courses through the integration of LMS.
 
Participation in the global innovative learning programmes would enable Armenia to:
 

Build upon existing initiatives with a comprehensive, system-wide approach

Align national efforts with global best practices and evidence-based solutions

Accelerate progress toward measurable learning outcomes with equity at the core

Strengthen the capacity of teachers through innovative tools and methodologies
 
I would greatly appreciate the opportunity to discuss Armenia's potential participation in the initial phase or subsequent phases of the Strategy's rollout. A meeting would allow us to:
 

Explore specific programme alignment with Armenia's education priorities

Discuss implementation modalities and timelines

Identify partnership opportunities and resource requirements

Determine next steps for formal engagement

shortDescription: Capacity building of UNICEF Pacific staff
description:
Last year marked the midpoint of UNICEF Pacific MCPD, and we conducted a deep-dive exercise of the climate programme. One of the key findings was that many colleagues do not yet feel sufficiently equipped to integrate climate considerations into their work, which is limiting the shift of our programmes toward climate resilience. A critical enabler of success is ensuring that UNICEF Pacific staff have the skills and tools needed to support programme design, implementation and resource mobilization, enabling a sustained transition toward climate-resilient programming.

We would therefore like to request support from the COE in the design and implementation of a training programme. The initial objective is to strengthen staff understanding of the basic science of climate change and its impacts on children, social services and UNICEF programmes, as well as the key frameworks that guide climate action, including adaptation, mitigation and loss and damage. The training would also aim to build practical skills on how to design climate- and risk-informed programming. 

We expect participation from all result areas. Given that our office operates across six locations in the Pacific Islands (one multi-country office and five field offices), the training may need to be delivered through more than one session. We would also hope for the training to be highly practical and action-oriented, supporting teams to apply the concepts directly to their programme areas.

shortDescription: Enhance water security for last-mile Afghan households through climate-adaptive, snowmelt-based solutions
description:
Technical assistance to design climate-resilient water security solutions for vulnerable households in hard-to-reach mountainous and snow-covered areas of Afghanistan in the context of a rapidly changing climate context. This includes multidisciplinary expertise in climate scenario development, hydrogeology, water recharge systems modelling, and innovative technologies and indigenous knowledge for rain and snowmelt harvesting for water security.
 
Technical assistance will lead to a strategy that will guide interventions, measure water access outcomes, strengthen evidence-based programming at scale, ensuring sustainability, resilience, and reduced vulnerability to climate variability for the most affected and marginalized communities.
objectives:
Comprehensive assessment report of snowmelt-dependent and groundwater-depleted areas in Afghanistan to inform targeted interventions. (Q1 – 2026)

Technical designs and guidelines for small-scale water storage and harvesting systems, and recharge technologies adapted to hard-to-reach areas. (Q2 – Q3 2026)

Tools and pathways to measure household water security outcomes and guide evidence-based scaling of interventions. (Q4 – 2026)
